body:
Thanks for finding this bug, and also I have to say I really enjoyed [your blog post](https://www.ryanliptak.com/blog/better-named-character-reference-tokenization/).

I worry a bit that the new error description is too precise and implementer-focused, instead of fitting the role of the error names table which is to tell web developers what they are doing wrong when the parser gives a certain error. From this perspective, you can kind of see what the previous description was trying to get at, although it was technically wrong. It was probably trying to say something like "If you write `&notin` with no semicolon, that's ambiguous between `¬in` and `∉`, so you're gonna get an error. Add the semicolon appropriately to reduce the ambiguity."

Can you think of a way of revising this description/example which focuses on this point? I worry that the new text you've proposed is mostly focused on reproducing the parser behavior in two places in the spec, instead of steering authors in the right direction to avoid ambiguity.

Thanks, happy to hear it!

To me, describing `&notin` as ambiguous is a bit strange, since it's exactly as ambiguous as `&notabcdef` or `&not1234` (that is, none of them is in the named character references table). Is the intention to provide an example that *is* ambiguous (e.g. `&foobar` if both `&foo` and `&foobar` were in the named character references table without a semicolon)? If so, there is no actual case where that's true: no named character reference without a semicolon is a substring of another named character reference without a semicolon. I mostly agree that my current description might be too precise. My inclination, though, would be to just delete everything after the first two sentences, i.e. make the description just:

> This error occurs if the parser encounters a character reference that is not terminated by a U+003B (;) code point. The parser behaves the same as if the character reference is terminated by the U+003B (;) code point.

Maybe invert it? ```

For example, &notin will be parsed as "¬in", i.e., the same as if the input were ¬in, whereas ∉ will be parsed as "∉".

```

> To me, describing `&notin` as ambiguous is a bit strange, since it's exactly as ambiguous as `&notabcdef` or `&not1234` (that is, none of them is in the named character references table).

I think the difference is that most web developers don't know about the named character reference table, and just have a vague sense "sometimes the `&stuff;` syntax works when I leave off the trailing `;`". So this hypothetical web developer might be used to `&not` or `&amp` or `&nbsp` working, and thus expect `&notin` to work in the same way.

The purpose of the error is to tell developers: stop doing that. Always include the `;`. Even if the browser happens to recognize the reference (because it's in this mysterious hard-coded table all the browsers ship), this isn't the right way to code. Just always include the `;`.

Thanks for clarifying, that makes sense. Tried to reword the note with that in mind, and used @annevk's inverted example since it fits better with the intended idea.

EDIT: At this point, could also keep the description as-it-was before this PR, delete the note, and just update the example. Let me know if that'd be preferred.
